title: Calls grow for audit of Labor finances
full_text:
The former Kennett government’s Victorian commission of audit chief, Saul Eslake, and other prominent economists have added to calls for an audit of the federal government’s finances, despite Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino playing down the need.
Past commissioners and executives of the last national audit called for a fresh review of the Albanese government’s finances this week after official figures revealed government spending had hit 26.9 per cent of GDP, above the May budget forecast, and that policy decisions in Labor’s past eight budget updates had not led to “net savings”.
“I certainly wouldn’t call it DOGE,” Mr Eslake said, referring to Elon Musk’s short-lived US cost-cutting attempt, “but there is a useful role for a bunch of outsiders to run the ruler over federal agencies and programs.” Mr Eslake said an independent review last year of the Victorian public service by former secretary of the Department of Premier and Cabinet, Helen Silver, would now be useful at the federal level.
Mr Eslake, who served as executive for the Victorian Commission of Audit in 1993, said that given pre-election economic and fiscal outlooks had become common, such reviews could no longer be used by a new government as an excuse to claim that previous governments had left unreasonable financial challenges, but an audit could still be used to help a government make cuts that it wanted the public to support.
“It has been apparent since Covid that government spending as a percentage of GDP is about 2 per cent higher than it was before, and that’s because of the public demand for health, aged care and childcare, as well as defence spending and growing interest bill,” he said.
High levels of government spending have been recognised by economists and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock as a driver of higher than expected inflation.
After annual headline and core inflation rose by more than expected this week, financial markets have tipped an 80 per cent chance that the RBA will lift rates at its meeting next week, taking the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest level in 18 years.
While higher RBA interest rates apply pressure to the private sector and household spending, the central bank has not given any advice on the level of government spending.
Coles CEO Leah Weckert, who revealed a rare profit downgrade for the supermarkets operator on Friday blamed on rising costs, said household finances were feeling the pressure. “Certainly what we are hearing from them is that their budgets at home are stretched, and that they are very deliberately taking actions to seek out ways to lower the cost of pretty much every line that they have in the household budget,” Ms Weckert said.
The ANZ-Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence index slipped in October, with the net number of households thinking it’s a good time to buy a major household item falling 10 points to -17 per cent.
While other economists have also backed an audit of government finances, Dr Mulino dismissed it on Friday.
“I remember when the Abbott government had an audit, and look where that led to in terms of actual outcomes,” Dr Mulino said. “There are no plans for that style of audit, and we’re delivering outcomes on fiscally responsible management through our budget and MYEFO processes.” Opposition Treasury spokesman Tim Wilson said Jim Chalmers didn’t need a commission of audit “because we’ve already outlined $31.3bn in savings to get spending down and take pressure off inflation”.
“The problem is this taxaholic Treasurer can’t kick his spending addiction, so there has to be a point where the Prime Minister needs to sack his Treasurer, who has raised the white flag to higher inflation and interest rates,” Mr Wilson said.
AMP chief economist Shane Oliver backed the need for commission of audit, saying it was “long overdue”.
“It’s the sort of thing [former prime minister Paul] Keating would have done,” Dr Oliver said. “Keating went into a winter election in 1987 promising spending cuts and they won because he sold the story so well – he told the truth. That’s how he was able to cut so efficiently in the 1980s.” He said the focus should be looking at where to cut spending. “We really don’t have a revenue problem,” he said. “The problem is Australia’s excess levels of spending as a percentage of GDP. Since the GFC there has been increasing dependence on government and therefore governments are now expected to solve our problems – but there needs to be better communications to change that.” EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy said an audit was a good idea and should be conducted across all tiers of government.
“A commission of audit would be a positive step towards addressing Australia’s structural budget deficits and could help slow the accumulation of debt and restore more sustainable fiscal settings,” Ms Murphy said.
“It should examine spending across all levels of government, given gross public debt is expected to rise and exceed $2 trillion by the 2030 financial year.” She said greater scrutiny, supported by better data and AI-enabled analytics, could strengthen decision-making and deliver better outcomes for taxpayers.
KPMG chief economist Brendan Rynne said he would not ask for a formalised audit as such, but said a review would be worthwhile. “I think the experience with the Shepherd Review is that such reviews become too political, which reduces their value once vested interests become too publicly engaged with the process,” Dr Rynne said.
“However, I am suggesting the government do a simpler, behind the scenes line-by-line critical assessment of all programs and projects to ascertain their need.
“My suspicion is that there are a whole lot of legacy programs that are still active and remain past their used-by date.”
